title: Gathering the hymns
hookLine: with Bhai Gurdas as scribe, he gathers the Gurus' hymns and those of other saints into one book

cards: A grandmother's lullaby. The hymn at every funeral. The tune someone hums in the kitchen.
Songs like these often live only in people, and when the people go, verses slip away, words drift, and sometimes someone adds a verse of their own and passes it off as the old one.
By the time of Guru Arjan, the Sikh community had four Gurus' worth of hymns, sung every day, copied in handwritten books kept by different families.
And tradition says others were writing hymns in Guru Nanak's name that he never wrote. Guru Arjan decided the words needed one home.

teach.h: GURU ARJAN DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.
teach.b: Tradition says that around 1603, at a quiet spot by a pool near Amritsar, Guru Arjan sat down to make a book. His scribe was Bhai Gurdas, a scholar and poet, the Guru's relative, whose own verses Sikhs still read.
The Guru dictated; Bhai Gurdas wrote. First, he gathered.
Earlier Gurus' hymns had been collected in handwritten volumes under the third Guru, and tradition says those books were kept by his son, Baba Mohan, who would not hand them over.
So Guru Arjan went to his house and sang outside his window, a hymn in his honor, until Mohan came down and gave them up.

teach.h: SORTED BY RAGA, LIKE A SONGBOOK.
teach.b: Second, he sorted: not by author or by date, but by raga, the musical mode each hymn was meant to be sung in, so the book is laid out like a songbook for the day and its moods.
Third, the surprise: he opened the book to others.

teach.h: KABIR, RAVIDAS, FARID ON ONE PAGE.
teach.b: Beside the Gurus' words he placed hymns by saints from outside the Sikh community: Kabir, a weaver from Benares; Namdev, a calico printer; Ravidas, a leatherworker whom his society called untouchable; and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi who had lived centuries before.
Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, on the same pages; Sikhs understand it as the Guru hearing in them the same truth about the one God.
And he left some things out: the hymns written falsely in Nanak's name did not go in. Gather, sort, open the pages, and guard them. That's how a scattered songbook became one book.

how: Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as the compiler of the Adi Granth, the book that became the Guru Granth Sahib, and the hymns of Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid and other saints are sung in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own.

practice: Let your mind go looking, the way the Guru went looking: a line someone said that you've never forgotten, a recipe only one person in your family knows, a song, a joke, a piece of advice.
Pick one, and picture where it lives right now: in one person's head, on a scrap of paper, in a phone that could break. Hold it a while, and ask where it would be safe.

wordCard.voice: Raag. The musical mode Guru Arjan used to sort the gathered hymns, so the scripture reads like a songbook for the day and its moods.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a raga, the musical mode that orders the hymns of the book.
